content: Respiratory viral infections in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) significantly impair lung function and contribute to the progression of their disease. As a result, annual influenza vaccination is frequently recommended for this population to mitigate these risks. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of influenza vaccination in individuals with CF. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register. This register includes references obtained from extensive electronic database searches, manual searches of relevant journals, and conference proceedings. Additionally, vaccine manufacturers were contacted to gather further information on randomized controlled trials. The most recent search of the register was performed on July 8, 2013. The review included all randomized and quasi-randomized trials, whether published or unpublished, that compared any influenza vaccine to either a placebo or another type of influenza vaccine. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. When necessary, additional information was obtained by directly contacting the investigators. Four studies, involving a total of 179 participants with CF, were included in the review. Of these participants, 143 (80%) were children aged between 1 and 16 years. None of the studies compared an influenza vaccine to a placebo, nor did they compare a whole virus vaccine to a subunit or split virus vaccine. Two studies compared a live attenuated intranasal vaccine to an inactivated intramuscular vaccine. The other two studies compared a split virus vaccine to a subunit vaccine and a virosome vaccine to a subunit vaccine, all administered intramuscularly. The incidence of adverse events varied depending on the type of influenza vaccine used, but it was generally high. The overall rate of adverse events ranged from 24% (48 out of 201 participants) for the intranasal live vaccine to 43% (13 out of 30 participants) for the split virus vaccine. However, none of the adverse events reported were severe. Due to the limited statistical power of the studies, no significant differences were observed between the various vaccines in terms of adverse event rates. All the vaccines studied elicited a satisfactory serological antibody response. However, none of the studies reported any other clinically significant benefits of vaccination. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence from randomized studies to support the benefit of influenza vaccination in individuals with CF. They emphasized the need for a well-designed clinical trial to evaluate the effectiveness of influenza vaccination on meaningful clinical outcomes in this population.
